rules.title: Explicit column lists
rules.what: SELECT names its columns; INSERT names its columns; never SELECT * or column-less INSERT on tables that can grow or evolve.
rules.why: SELECT * transfers every column including the ones added later that the code never wanted; a column-less INSERT breaks the day the schema gains a column.
rules.how: List the columns the code reads in SELECT and INSERT statements; keep the list in sync at schema reviews.

patterns.note: Column-less INSERT; breaks on schema change.

verify.how: No unmasked SELECT * / column-less INSERT in reviewed statements.

limits: EXISTS probes and interactive exploration are the documented exceptions.

rules.title: JOINs over correlated subqueries on growing data
rules.what: Prefer joins and derived tables over correlated subqueries inside SELECT/WHERE on large tables; verify with the query plan.
rules.why: A correlated subquery can execute once per outer row: O(outer x inner) where a join is a single pass. The plan, not intuition, decides.
rules.how: Rewrite as joins/CTEs, check EXPLAIN for row estimates and access types, keep the plan output with the change.

patterns.note: Correlated subquery in WHERE; verify row counts and plan.

verify.how: EXPLAIN before/after: execution time and rows examined on a realistic dataset.

limits: Small lookup tables make correlated subqueries perfectly fine; the plan decides.

rules.title: Batch inserts, not row-by-row loops
rules.what: Bulk loads use multi-row INSERT / COPY / batch APIs, not one INSERT per row in a loop.
rules.why: Each single-row INSERT pays a round trip, a parse and a transaction; a batched one amortises all three across thousands of rows.
rules.how: Multi-row VALUES, executemany with a real batch, COPY on Postgres, keep the batch size bounded.

patterns.note: Single-row INSERT; candidate if emitted from a loop by the calling code - see language rules.

verify.how: Load time per N rows within budget; round trips counted.

rules.title: No function on the indexed column in predicates
rules.what: WHERE clauses do not wrap the indexed column in a function (WHERE lower(email) = ?, WHERE DATE(created_at) = ?); use expression indexes or range predicates instead.
rules.why: Wrapping the column in a function defeats the index: the database falls back to a scan that grows with the table on every execution.
rules.how: Normalise at write time, create an expression index for the exact function, or rewrite as a range (created_at >= ? AND < ?+1d); verify with EXPLAIN.

patterns.note: Function on a column in a predicate; candidate for index-defeating predicate - check the plan.

verify.how: EXPLAIN shows index usage on the rewritten predicate.

limits: Expression indexes exist precisely for this; their cost is recorded like any index (NR-DATA-003).

rules.title: Transactions short and bounded
rules.what: Transactions contain the database work and nothing else: no external calls inside a transaction, no user-wait inside one, and their scope is explicit.
rules.why: A transaction holding locks across an HTTP call or a user think-time blocks every concurrent writer on the same rows: the service's write throughput collapses on one slow dependency.
rules.how: Open late, commit early, keep external calls outside the transaction boundary; use explicit BEGIN/COMMIT rather than implicit autocommit chains.

verify.how: Lock-wait metrics under load within budget; transaction duration p99 within the stated bound.

rules.title: Keyset pagination instead of deep OFFSET
rules.what: Paginate large result sets by key (WHERE id > :last ORDER BY id LIMIT n), not by OFFSET.
rules.why: OFFSET n reads and discards n rows at every page: the deeper the page, the more work for nothing.
rules.how: Keep the last key of the page; index the ORDER BY columns; OFFSET stays fine for small, bounded lists.

patterns.note: OFFSET with a large or variable value.

verify.how: Plan of a deep page shows an index range scan, not a scan of the skipped rows.

rules.title: No DISTINCT to hide a bad join
rules.what: Use DISTINCT only when duplicates are inherent to the question; fix the join (or use EXISTS) when it multiplies rows.
rules.why: DISTINCT over a fanned-out join sorts or hashes the whole intermediate result to remove rows that should never have been produced.
rules.how: Replace join + DISTINCT with WHERE EXISTS (...) or aggregate before joining.

patterns.note: DISTINCT with a join: check for row fan-out.

verify.how: Each DISTINCT is justified by the data model, not by the join.

rules.title: Commit and purge in bounded batches
rules.what: Commit in batches sized to undo/redo capacity, never per row; delete or archive large volumes in bounded chunks, never one giant statement.
rules.why: A commit per row multiplies log flushes; one massive DELETE holds locks, bloats undo and replication, and can stall the whole database.
rules.how: Loop over batches of a few thousand rows with a checkpoint; partition and drop old partitions where the engine supports it.

patterns.note: Unfiltered DELETE of a whole table; check volume, or TRUNCATE/partition drop.

verify.how: Batch job test shows commits proportional to batches; purge run on a copy stays within the lock budget.

rules.title: Types sized to the data
rules.what: Choose column types from the data's real range (varchar(n), integer widths, date not timestamp-as-text); avoid VARCHAR(MAX)/CLOB by default.
rules.why: Oversized types inflate rows, indexes, memory grants and backups, multiplied by every row and every replica.
rules.how: Pick the narrowest correct type; store dates as dates; reserve LOB types for genuinely large content.

patterns.note: Unbounded text type; check it is needed.

verify.how: Schema review records the expected range of each wide column.

rules.title: No row-by-row logging in production code
rules.what: Do not leave per-row trace output (DBMS_OUTPUT, RAISE NOTICE, PRINT in loops) in production procedures.
rules.why: Per-row output costs CPU and memory buffers on every run, for messages nobody reads.
rules.how: Log aggregates once per batch; gate debug output behind a parameter.

patterns.note: Trace output; check it is not per row in production.

verify.how: Production procedures contain no per-row trace output.
